blocks.text: Claude Docs 向公众开放前三周，它还只是一个概念验证，跑在单个节点上，只有 Anthropic 内部几千人在用。当时我们正赶一个野心不小的上线日期，而按我们自己的估算，上线头几天就会产生数百万份文档。

inlines.text: Claude Docs 向公众开放前三周，它还只是一个概念验证，跑在单个节点上，只有 Anthropic 内部几千人在用。当时我们正赶一个野心不小的上线日期，而按我们自己的估算，上线头几天就会产生数百万份文档。

blocks.text: 我们在 9 月 16 日上线。到 9 月 22 日，用户已经创建了超过 460 万份文档。在 20 亿次请求中，我们只看到 60 次服务器错误，而且全程没有回滚过。整个 Docs 服务跑在大约 50 个内存优化型 pod 上。

inlines.text: 我们在 9 月 16 日上线。到 9 月 22 日，用户已经创建了超过 460 万份文档。在 20 亿次请求中，我们只看到 60 次服务器错误，而且全程没有回滚过。整个 Docs 服务跑在大约 50 个内存优化型 pod 上。

blocks.text: 靠的是两个决定：

inlines.text: 靠的是两个决定：
在上线规模下跑混沌循环。
我们在预发布环境搭了一套测试框架，让 Claude 连续跑了两周，专门想办法把服务搞垮。它对基础设施的每个部分都做了压力测试，哪里扛不住就修哪里。
让 Claude 更容易看懂。
只有当系统在每一轮迭代中都产出准确的遥测数据，Claude 才能有效地把修复闭环跑起来。我们很早就做了一个决定：避开那些会以代码难以控制的方式占用内存或 CPU 的运行时（比如带垃圾回收的运行时）。这样当某个遥测信号看起来不对劲时，Claude 就能轻松追到某个 bug 或某个具体的设计决策上。

blocks.text: 但说实话，这事能成，主要还是因为我们的前沿模型最近进步很大（我用的是一个内部研究模型，大致相当于 Claude Fable 5.2）。在我们的经验里，它们现在能在一个像这样的任务里盯住同一个目标好几周，这正是我们能在紧张的时间表里撑到上线规模的原因。

blocks.text: 一台机器上几千个内部用户，根本说明不了服务能不能扛住上线，而我们显然也没有上线流量可以用来测试。

blocks.text: 我们需要真实证据来判断能多快放量。所以在 9 月 4 日，也就是上线前大约两周，我让 Claude 去驱动一个与生产环境镜像的预发布集群，每天造出超过一百万份合成文档，并故意打坏核心组件。然后……我就让它一直跑着（完整成本我放在文末了）。

blocks.text: 我的设置很简单。这个循环就是 Claude Code 里一个我一直开着的会话：选一个场景，跑测试框架，读遥测，提出修复方案，部署到预发布环境，重复。这个会话充当协调者，把大部分工作交给子智能体。最忙的一周，通常同时有大约 11 个子智能体在跑，峰值到过 30 个。协调者还通过 Slack MCP 跟我们内部的 Claude Tag（beta）变体对话，向 Anthropic 内部其他扩展过类似服务的基础设施团队取经。他们的智能体帮我们检查扩展方案，看有没有他们踩过的坑。

blocks.text: 如果建议容易回退，Claude 就写好改动、部署到预发布环境，再重跑测试。服务执行的每个操作都有遥测。比如每条数据库查询都会报告自己的名字、扫描了多少行、返回了多少行，这样 Claude 就能发现烂查询并重写它。

Top row, left to right: the harness adds load, Claude reads the telemetry, Claude proposes options, and you pick one. Inside the loop: opens instantly, and check that no confirmed edit was lost.

inlines.text: 对我们来说，结果就是一个能扛住发布的服务。为了达到这个目标，我们做了两件事，让服务尽可能对 Claude 清晰可读：
诊断循环。

清晰可读的技术选型。

blocks.text: 在测试框架运行的早期，有一份大文档在其 pod 上占用了约 3 GB（这数字可不好看）。Claude 第一次尝试修复时，是缩小我们的一个缓存，让服务器更早地驱逐文档。下一次测试框架运行显示，内存实际上在一个单独的缓存里，位于我们的某个依赖项内部，于是 Claude 撤回了那个改动。

blocks.text: 我们对服务的运行时和依赖很挑剔。我们希望 Claude 测量的任何东西都能追溯到我们写的代码。

inlines.text: 我们对服务的运行时和依赖很挑剔。我们希望 Claude 测量的任何东西都能追溯到我们写的代码。

blocks.text: 这是因为我们的模型在信号干净时爬山效果最好。我们预计垃圾回收器会带来噪声，因为内存和延迟会随回收器的调度而波动。

inlines.text: 这是因为我们的模型在信号干净时爬山效果最好。我们预计垃圾回收器会带来噪声，因为内存和延迟会随回收器的调度而波动。

blocks.text: 有两个选择帮助最大。

inlines.text: 有两个选择帮助最大。
我们用 Rust 写了这个服务
。没有垃圾回收器，一个文档的所有内存都放在我们自己定义的结构里，所以当内存增长时，Claude 能指出是哪一处造成的，改掉它，再看下一轮迭代内存有没有降下来。Anthropic 的 Go 工具链也很好，我们并没有对两种语言做对比评测，所以这只是我们在 Rust 上的经验。我过去写过 Go，这次让我欣赏的一点是：代码用完某块内存之后，我几乎不用去想它还会不会一直占着。
我们还把依赖压到了最少
。每个库都会带来我们没写过、也不容易说清楚的数据结构。对少数确实需要的库，我们把代码 vendor 进来，这样就能自己读、自己测。

blocks.text: Rust 写起来对人很难，几年前这会严重影响选型。现在 Claude 写 Rust 和写大多数其他语言都没问题，这一点就没那么重要了。

inlines.text: Rust 写起来对人很难，几年前这会严重影响选型。现在 Claude 写 Rust 和写大多数其他语言都没问题，这一点就没那么重要了。

blocks.alt: We wanted every number to trace back to code we wrote, so we used Rust and kept dependencies to a minimum. Two lanes. What we chose: Rust and few dependencies, so memory sits in our own structures, then Claude finds the cause, then fixes are easy to check. What we avoided, a bet and not a test: garbage collection and libraries we didn't write, then memory we can't account for, then a noisier signal that is harder to trace to our code.

blocks.text: 发布周有种奇怪的熟悉感。Claude 很擅长设想一个服务会怎么失败，而且早在发布前就把大多数情况规划好了。我们在预发环境演练过的十个场景里，有七个真的在生产环境发生了。到那时，测试框架已经让预发环境把大部分情况都跑过一遍，Claude 也把修复放在运行时开关后面发布出去了。基础设施某部分吃紧时，我们通常只要拨一下开关。

blocks.text: 关于成本有几点要说：

inlines.text: 关于成本有几点要说：
我们的发布规模特别大。
相当一部分钱花在了只有这个规模才说得通的基础设施上，而理解这些基础设施本身又需要更多推理。Claude 得花更多心思去想，一组不断增长的服务如何协同工作，以及它们可能以哪些方式失败。

blocks.text: Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days.

inlines.text: Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days.

blocks.text: We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods.

inlines.text: We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods.

blocks.text: Two decisions got us there:

inlines.text: Two decisions got us there:
A chaos loop at launch scale.

We set up a test harness on our staging environment where Claude ran constantly for two weeks to try and break the service. It load tested every part of our infrastructure and fixed whatever fell over.
Improving legibility to Claude.

Claude could only close the loop effectively on fixes if our system produced accurate telemetry every iteration. We made a call early to avoid any runtime that uses memory or CPU in ways our code can't easily control (e.g. runtimes with garbage collection). When a telemetry signal looked concerning, Claude could easily trace it to a bug or a specific design decision.

blocks.text: But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline.

blocks.text: THE CHAOS LOOP

inlines.text: THE CHAOS LOOP

blocks.text: A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with.

inlines.text: A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with.

blocks.text: We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article).

inlines.text: We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article).

blocks.text: My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit.

blocks.text: The fun part was picking scenarios I thought were paranoid:

inlines.text: The fun part was picking scenarios I thought were paranoid:
10M new docs created in a single day
22,000 live connections reconnecting at once
One hot doc with hundreds of viewers, a server killed while it was still loading a doc, and the database stalling

blocks.text: Each iteration looked the same. Our testing harness selected a feature like document creation and pushed creation to saturation. Claude then read telemetry using the Datadog MCP and came back with a short menu of options and a recommendation.

inlines.text: Each iteration looked the same. Our testing harness selected a feature like document creation and pushed creation to saturation. Claude then read telemetry using the Datadog MCP and came back with a short menu of options and a recommendation.

blocks.text: If the recommendation was easy to undo, Claude wrote and deployed the change to staging and reran the test. We had telemetry on every operation the service ran. Every database query, for example, reported its name and how many rows it scanned versus how many it returned, so Claude could spot a bad query and rewrite it.

inlines.text: MAKING THE SERVICE LEGIBLE TO CLAUDE

blocks.text: My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with models. His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task.

outcome

blocks.text: So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix.

inlines.text: So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix.

blocks.text: For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could:

inlines.text: For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could:
A diagnostic loop.
Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing.
Legible technology choices.
We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote.

blocks.text: A diagnostic loop

inlines.text: A diagnostic loop

blocks.text: Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes.

inlines.text: Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes.

blocks.text: Memory is the best example.

inlines.text: Memory is the best example.

blocks.text: Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change.

inlines.text: Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a
separate
cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change.

blocks.text: From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy.

inlines.text: From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy.

blocks.text: After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what we’d need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50.

blocks.alt: Claude adds telemetry as it goes. A loop of six steps: the harness stresses the service, the service reports telemetry, and Claude reads it and traces it to a cause. Then Claude adds what's missing, which is highlighted, Claude fixes it or drops a wrong guess, and Claude deploys and reruns, with hard-to-undo changes going to you first, which leads back to the harness.

blocks.text: Legible technology choices

inlines.text: Legible technology choices

blocks.text: We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote.

inlines.text: We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote.

blocks.text: This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule.

inlines.text: This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule.

blocks.text: Two choices helped the most.

inlines.text: Two choices helped the most.
We wrote the service in Rust

. With no garbage collector, all of a doc’s memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didn’t bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it.
We also kept dependencies to a minimum
. Every library brings data structures we didn’t write and can’t easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves.

blocks.text: Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now.

inlines.text: Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now.

blocks.alt: We wanted every number to trace back to code we wrote, so we used Rust and kept dependencies to a minimum. Two lanes. What we chose: Rust and few dependencies, so memory sits in our own structures, then Claude finds the cause, then fixes are easy to check. What we avoided, a bet and not a test: garbage collection and libraries we didn't write, then memory we can't account for, then a noisier signal that is harder to trace to our code.

blocks.text: The service held at launch scale. The first million docs showed up in about 30 hours, and we were past 4.6 million by September 22. We rolled prod 629 times in September and never once rolled back.

inlines.text: The service held at launch scale. The first million docs showed up in about 30 hours, and we were past 4.6 million by September 22. We rolled prod 629 times in September and never once rolled back.

blocks.text: Launch week felt weirdly familiar. Claude is great at imagining ways a service can fail and had planned for most of them well before launch. Seven of the ten scenarios we’d rehearsed on staging actually happened in prod. By then the harness had already put staging through most of it, and Claude had shipped the fixes behind runtime flags. When part of the infra ran into pressure, we usually just flipped a flag.

Other Anthropic employees have called this goal drift.

blocks.text: A couple of things about the cost:

inlines.text: A couple of things about the cost:
Our launch was particularly massive.

A good chunk of the money went into infrastructure that only makes sense at that scale, and that infrastructure took more inference to reason about. Claude had to think a lot harder about how a growing set of services fit together and all the ways they could fail.
I also burned a lot of tokens figuring out the process.
The loop ran nonstop while I was experimenting with the setup. Knowing what I know now, I think we could have spent about half as much.

Give Claude access to your telemetry. Most observability providers have an MCP server that Claude can use.

Have Claude write a load script that throws ten times your real traffic at the staging copy of the service and breaks things on purpose. Killing an instance, stalling the database, and deploying in the middle of a spike are good places to start. Then let Claude keep fixing whatever falls over.
When you’re picking your stack, lean toward whatever Claude can measure most easily. For us that was Rust and as few dependencies as possible.
Before you start, write down your most important technical invariants and give them to Claude.
